children.text: On a small island off Nasugbu stand Greek temple-style columns left behind by a luxury resort that closed in
, earning it the nickname "Greece in the Philippines." Here you can photograph the columns against the blue sea, go cliff diving, and camp on a deserted island.
Fortune Island is a small island of about 27 hectares, roughly
14km
west of the coast of Nasugbu, Batangas Province, with its highest point about
above sea level. Ringed by limestone cliffs, the island opens onto a white-sand beach on one side, and the surrounding waters shift vividly from jade to deep indigo as the depth changes.
What made the island famous are the Greek temple-style columns rising atop its cliffs. In

, former Batangas governor José Antonio Leviste opened an exclusive members-only resort here, the "Fortune Island Resort Club," complete with columns and statues modeled on the Acropolis of Athens, a saltwater pool, a helipad, and even an exhibition hall for artifacts from the galleon San Diego. But with no fresh water on the island, operating costs were high, and with typhoon damage on top of that, the resort closed in
. The long-abandoned ruins, blending with the sea, earned the nickname "Greece in the Philippines" and became a popular photo spot, and around
the island reopened to the general public. Today, Fortune Island Resort in Wawa village on the mainland handles registration and boats, running the island as a day-trip and camping destination.

Boats land at a white-sand beach on the island's southeast side, facing the mainland. Climb the stone steps up the hill at the beach's southern end to reach the Acropolis columns, while the old pool, villas, former helipad, and lion statues lie scattered behind the beach. At the island's summit stands a small unmanned lighthouse maintained by the Philippine Coast Guard, which you can reach in about
30 minutes
on foot along a rocky trail. Most visitors drop their bags on the beach, see the columns and ruins first, then fill the rest of the day with swimming and a walk up to the lighthouse.

Fortune Island is a "semi-deserted island" with almost no amenities. There's no electricity, drinking water, or restaurants, so you have to bring all your own food and drink, but that's exactly what makes a day on this island, far from the city, feel more special. Cliff diving, snorkeling, napping in a hammock, and camping under a sky full of stars — you can enjoy it all on this one island.

It suits travelers in their 20s and 30s coming with friends or clubs, photography travelers, and families who enjoy camping. Since you charter an entire boat, the more people in your group, the more the per-person cost drops. On the other hand, if you'd rather have a comfortable resort stay, it's better to stay at a beach resort on the Nasugbu mainland and visit as a day trip.
A view of the sea framed between the cliffside columns is the island's signature shot. It looks most three-dimensional before
9 AM
or after
4 PM
, when the sunlight comes in from the side.
Leap into deep water from various points along the island's coastal cliffs; the highest spots are about
. Only attempt it if you're a confident swimmer and have a life vest ready.
There's coral and tropical fish just off the beach and below the cliffs. There can be currents, so it's safer to snorkel close to the beach.
Walk a loop around the island past the old resort's former pool site, staircases, and traces of statues.
30–40 minutes
is enough to see all the main spots.
The beach on the east side of the island has fine sand and clear water, great for swimming. Shade is scarce, so bringing a tarp or parasol makes it more comfortable.

blocks.title: Camping and stargazing on a deserted island

children.text: Stay overnight and you get the quiet island all to yourself once the day-trip crowds have left. With no light pollution, you can sometimes even see the Milky Way on a clear night.
From the cliffs on the island's west side, you can watch the sun set over the South China Sea, and from the beach, see it rise over the mountains of mainland Batangas. Walk about
30 minutes
up to the lighthouse at the summit for a sweeping view of the whole island and the Nasugbu coast.

blocks.title: The story of the galleon San Diego

children.text: About
northwest of the island, on the seabed, lies the Spanish galleon San Diego, which sank on
December 14, 1600
while fighting Dutch warships. It was discovered in
at a depth of about
, and more than 34,000 artifacts, including Ming dynasty blue-and-white porcelain and cannons, were salvaged; they are now on display at the
National Museum of the Philippines
(National Museum of Anthropology) in Manila. Look out over that sea from the island and imagine the story from more than 400 years ago.

In Manila, catch a bus to Nasugbu (DLTB, San Agustin, St. Gabriel, etc.) from the DLTB terminal in Buendia, Pasay (near LRT Gil Puyat Station), the Genesis terminal below MRT Taft Avenue Station, or PITX in Parañaque. The ride takes about
3–4 hours
and costs about
. From Nasugbu town, a tricycle to Fortune Island Resort (dock and management office) in Barangay Wawa takes
10–15 minutes
and costs about
per person on a shared ride.
DLTB's Buendia route runs roughly every hour, from the first bus at
3–4 AM
until around
8 PM

. St. Gabriel buses take the coastal road through the Kaybiang Tunnel in Ternate, Cavite. On Friday afternoons and Saturdays, traffic backs up on Aguinaldo Highway in Cavite and around Tagaytay, so the trip takes longer; if you want to catch the first boat, take the first bus before dawn.
From Manila, take the Coastal Road south into Cavite and continue via the Tagaytay–Nasugbu Highway, or take SLEX through Santa Rosa up to Tagaytay and then head down to Nasugbu. It's about
and takes
2.5–3.5 hours
. There's paid parking around Wawa dock.

Taking the Ternate–Nasugbu coastal road from Ternate, Cavite, through the Kaybiang Tunnel lets you enjoy sea views on the way down to Nasugbu. If you park at Fortune Island Resort in Wawa, parking for a car costs
for a day trip and
overnight.
Rent a bangka at Wawa dock and travel about
1–1.5 hours
. Round-trip bangka fares are set by group size: on a day-trip basis about
for up to 8 people, about
for 9–12 people, and about

for up to 25 people, and an overnight stay costs a little more. If camping overnight, arrange the pickup time for the next day in advance and get the captain's mobile phone number. The island entrance fee is paid separately at the dock office.
A day-trip round trip for 13–15 people costs
, while an overnight round trip costs
for up to 8 people,
for 13–15, and

for 16–25. Registration and all payments are handled at Fortune Island Resort on Apacible Boulevard in Wawa; visitors 6 and older pay the adult rate, and children 5 and under enter free. Rates may change, so check the latest prices with the resort.
Joiner tours bundling Manila pickup, boat, and entrance fee are sold for about
per person. For travelers in a small group, a joiner tour is far more economical.
Joiner tours usually leave Manila (from around MOA in Pasay, among other pickup points) by van at around
3 AM
and return around
7 PM

, and many only depart once a minimum number of participants (about 12) has signed up. Private tours, where a group of 2–4 has the vehicle to itself, cost much more per person, so for a small group a joiner tour or the bus is the better choice.

items.title: From the airport or other starting points

children.text: If you land at Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA), the simplest option is to take a taxi or Grab to nearby PITX and catch a bus to Nasugbu there. From Tagaytay, DLTB and San Agustin buses bound for Nasugbu can be caught around Olivarez, and the ride takes about
1–1.5 hours
. From Batangas City, BSC buses run to Nasugbu, and from Balayan to the south you can get there by jeepney via Tuy.
The best time to visit is the dry season,
November–May
, and within that the ideal stretch is
March–May

, when the sea is calmest and the water clearest. Conditions for cliff diving and snorkeling are also at their best then. However, with little shade on the island, it feels extremely hot at midday, so sun protection is a must. In
April
, the hottest month, daytime highs climb to around
From
December–February
, the northeast monsoon can bring stronger afternoon winds and waves, but the cooler temperatures actually make it pleasant for camping. During the
June–October

rainy season, the southwest monsoon (habagat) blows straight in off the western sea, kicking up high waves, and when a typhoon warning is issued, the coast guard bans boat trips. In the rainy season, be sure to check with the management office the day before whether boats are running. Rain is heaviest in
July–August
, with monthly rainfall reaching 400–500mm. In
August 2026

, heavy southwest monsoon rains led to a state of calamity being declared in Nasugbu, and the municipal tourism office suspended outdoor tourism, including boat trips and island tours, for days at a time.
During Holy Week and summer vacation weekends (
April–May
), the island gets crowded and boat waits get longer. If you want to photograph the columns without people around, take the first boat on a weekday morning, or camp overnight.

There are no hotels on the island; you can only camp in a tent or a rentable hut (cottage). If you want a comfortable stay, base yourself at a beach resort on the Nasugbu mainland coast and visit the island as a day trip. Along the Nasugbu coast, options range from simple beach resorts at about
a night to large resorts at

or more, and staying near Wawa dock or in Nasugbu town makes it easy to catch an early-morning boat. Fortune Island Resort in Wawa, which doubles as the boat dock, also has rooms with air conditioning and hot showers, at about
a night for a room for 2–3 people and about
for a room for 5–7. With the registration office and boats right out front, it's the most convenient place to stay for the first boat at dawn.

There are no restaurants or shops on the island, so you need to bring all your food. The usual approach is to buy grilled pork belly (liempo), roast chicken (lechon manok), rice, fruit, and ice at the public market or a big supermarket (Walter Mart) in Nasugbu town and pack it all in a cooler. Plan on at least 2–3 liters of water per person.

After you're back, treat yourself to grilled fish, squid, and sinigang at a Nasugbu seafood restaurant, or ease your tired body with Batangas-style bulalo beef soup and lomi noodles. If you head back via Tagaytay, the highland restaurant row is famous for its bulalo.
There's no drinking water on the island. Bring plenty of water for drinking and cooking, and pack separate water for washing up.
Always bag your trash and take it back with you. The island management requires that all waste be carried out.
Shade is scarce, so bring a tarp or large umbrella, a wide-brimmed hat, a rash guard, and reef-safe sunscreen.
Mobile signal is weak and only reaches parts of the island. Fix the return boat's time and place clearly with the captain before you land.
Reaching the cliff with the columns requires climbing stairs and slopes. Enclosed aqua shoes are safer than sandals.
Boat fares can be negotiated somewhat, but check the official posted rate at the dock first. Weekdays and the off-season can be a little cheaper.
If camping, bring a headlamp, power bank, insect repellent, and sturdy wind-resistant tent stakes. The sea wind can be quite strong at night.
There are ATMs in Nasugbu town, but none around Wawa dock. Have all your money ready in cash.
Boats to the island run only between
6 AM and 3 PM
, and boats back from the island only between
7 AM and 4 PM
. If you arrive late, your time on the island shrinks greatly, so get to the dock early in the morning.
The island's toilets and showers are basic facilities where you scoop seawater with a dipper. Save the freshwater shower for a mainland resort after you return, and bring wet wipes and tissues.
Before cliff diving, always check the water depth and the landing spot, and jump one person at a time. Don't do it on days with strong currents or high waves.
There are no lifeguards stationed around the island. Wear a life vest if you're not a strong swimmer, and always keep an adult watching children.
The old resort structures have deteriorated and risk collapsing. Don't climb onto the columns or walls, and respect off-limits areas.
Always wear a life vest when boarding the bangka. Winds pick up in the afternoon and waves get higher, so head back before it's too late.
Watch for heatstroke and dehydration at midday. Never drink alcohol before cliff diving or swimming.
Island rules (visitor caps, permitted camping areas, fire restrictions, etc.) change frequently, so check the latest notices before you set off.
The Nasugbu municipal tourism office suspends boat trips and island tours for a day or two at a time during bad weather (this happened twice in
August 2026
as well). Before setting out, check the Facebook announcements of the tourism office and Fortune Island Resort, and use only licensed boats.
